articles.takeaway: Investor confidence in the region remains strong despite the fall-out from the Iran war, with efforts to diversify economies helping to shield them from the crisis, a senior World Economic Forum official has said.
body: Investor confidence in the region remains strong despite the fall-out from the Iran war, with efforts to diversify economies helping to shield them from the crisis, a senior World Economic Forum official has said.
Kelsey Goodman, head of Middle East and North Africa at the World Economic Forum (WEF), told The National that the region’s economic fundamentals remained solid despite geopolitical uncertainty.
Her comments come as the International Monetary Fund sharply downgraded its 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies amid the effects of the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Sheikh Hamdan meets World Economic Forum president to strengthen UAE partnership “There’s still widespread investor confidence in the region,” Ms Goodman said. “The fundamentals are solid even if the surrounding area is uncertain, but it calls for the need for dialogue and co-operation and hopefully a return to peace and resiliency in the region.” Speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai, which concluded on Thursday, Ms Goodman said efforts to diversify Gulf economies had helped them withstand recent shocks and would be crucial to their recovery.
“Diversification really is key, and the companies and the economies that have been able to have already built in diversity into their plan are the ones that have been most resilient," she said.

"Resiliency is something that you have to prepare for. It's not something that you can build only in times of crisis.” Foresight simulations were carried out at the meeting on Thursday, in which participants rehearsed responses to unfolding geopolitical and technological crises.

articles.headline: Abu Dhabi Exports AI Government Services Platform Globally
articles.dek: Abu Dhabi has launched TAMM Global to offer its AI-powered unified government services platform to international markets, building on the success of its domestic TAMM app.
articles.lead: Abu Dhabi has established TAMM Global, a new entity tasked with exporting the emirate's artificial intelligence-driven unified government services platform to countries around the world. The company was created under the directive of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council.
articles.takeaway: Abu Dhabi has launched TAMM Global to offer its AI-powered unified government services platform to international markets, building on the success of its domestic TAMM app.
body: Abu Dhabi has established TAMM Global, a new entity tasked with exporting the emirate's artificial intelligence-driven unified government services platform to countries around the world. The company was created under the directive of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi and Chairman of the Abu Dhabi Executive Council.

TAMM Global will be responsible for developing, managing, and delivering an integrated system of digital government services. It will own and operate specialized digital platforms and hold the associated intellectual property rights, allowing it to license the platform's architecture and implementation methodologies to international partners.

Ahmed Al Kuttab, chairman of the Department of Government Enablement – Abu Dhabi (DGE), stated that the TAMM platform has become essential for interactions between people, businesses, and the government since its inception in 2005. The launch of TAMM Global aims to leverage the capabilities proven effective and efficient in Abu Dhabi for governments seeking to improve their service delivery.

The existing TAMM platform in Abu Dhabi integrates over 1,200 public and private sector services through a single digital gateway. This integration reportedly saves users approximately nine visits to government service centers annually, equating to about 12 hours. Since the integration of AI, customer satisfaction has increased to 94.5 percent from 78 percent in 2022, and the cost of service provision has decreased by 30 percent.

As an independent private-sector company, TAMM Global will collaborate directly with governments, organizations, and institutions globally. This approach will enable foreign governments to adapt pre-built services and digital capabilities to their specific legal and regulatory frameworks, facilitating quicker deployment without the need to replicate the entire development process.

TAMM's international recognition has grown, with the platform being named the world's best e-government initiative at the UN-backed World Summit on the Information Society Prizes in 2025. This year, it also received the Government category award for Europe, the Middle East, and Asia at the Gartner Eye on Innovation Awards.

articles.headline: UAE Ministry of Foreign Trade Discusses Trade Strategy Amidst Global Uncertainty
articles.dek: Fahad Al Gergawi outlines the UAE's approach to maintaining trade flow, expanding economic partnerships, and mitigating risks from geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions.
articles.lead: The United Arab Emirates is actively working to maintain its position as a global trading hub despite a challenging international trade environment marked by geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions. Fahad Al Gergawi, Undersecretary at the UAE Ministry of Foreign Trade, shared insights into the nation's strategy.
articles.takeaway: Fahad Al Gergawi outlines the UAE's approach to maintaining trade flow, expanding economic partnerships, and mitigating risks from geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions.
body: The United Arab Emirates is actively working to maintain its position as a global trading hub despite a challenging international trade environment marked by geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions. Fahad Al Gergawi, Undersecretary at the UAE Ministry of Foreign Trade, shared insights into the nation's strategy.

During a discussion at the World Economic Forum in Dubai, Al Gergawi detailed how the UAE is responding to disruptions, including those stemming from the Iran conflict. The country is exploring the expansion of alternative trade corridors to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz.

The UAE is also focusing on its growing network of Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements. These agreements are designed to help businesses gain access to new markets, attract investment, and bolster economic resilience.

Al Gergawi highlighted the UAE's ongoing efforts to navigate a fragmented global trading landscape. This includes continuing negotiations with the European Union and forging new international partnerships. The Undersecretary emphasized that long-term planning and adaptability are key to the UAE's trade strategy and economic recovery.

body: Sharjah has introduced Najm, an artificial intelligence agent designed to help foreign investors quickly identify investment opportunities within the emirate. The platform, launched by the Sharjah FDI Office (Invest in Sharjah), aims to speed up business processes and attract more foreign direct investment.

In its initial phase, Najm will assist investors in locating industrial facilities and commercial real estate. This is facilitated through partnerships with property portals Bayut, Property Finder, and e-commerce platform Dubizzle, which will provide the AI agent with relevant data.

The development of Najm is intended to simplify the investment decision-making process by delivering crucial information to investors precisely when they need it. This initiative comes as Sharjah seeks to bolster its foreign direct investment figures amidst global geopolitical uncertainties.

Last year, Sharjah attracted Dh7.74 billion in foreign direct investment, marking an 8.8 percent annual increase. The number of FDI projects also saw a significant rise of 45 percent, reaching 142 developments.

Future phases of the Najm platform plan to expand its scope to include investment opportunities in the healthcare, education, and technology sectors, further broadening the range of available assets for global investors.

articles.headline: Louvre Abu Dhabi Exhibition Explores 1,000 Years of Indian Ocean History
articles.dek: The new exhibition, 'Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean,' showcases maritime trade and cultural exchange from antiquity to the 17th century, centering the Arabian Gulf's historical role.
articles.lead: Louvre Abu Dhabi has opened a new exhibition, "Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean," which delves into over a thousand years of maritime history. The exhibition, running from October 14, 2026, to February 14, 2027, highlights the extensive trade and cultural connections that linked communities across the Indian Ocean, from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China, and Southeast Asia.
articles.takeaway: The new exhibition, 'Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean,' showcases maritime trade and cultural exchange from antiquity to the 17th century, centering the Arabian Gulf's historical role.
body: Louvre Abu Dhabi has opened a new exhibition, "Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean," which delves into over a thousand years of maritime history. The exhibition, running from October 14, 2026, to February 14, 2027, highlights the extensive trade and cultural connections that linked communities across the Indian Ocean, from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China, and Southeast Asia.

Organized in collaboration with the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris, the exhibition features approximately 240 artworks and historical objects. These include archaeological finds, jewelry, religious artifacts, and items recovered from shipwrecks, illustrating the flow of goods such as spices, precious stones, and textiles.

The exhibition emphasizes the central role of the Arabian Gulf in these historical networks, presenting the region's story from its perspective. It explores how commerce and spiritual exchange fostered relationships, citing the Arabian Gulf's pearl industry as a key example, with pearls traveling to India and beyond.

Visitors can explore navigational instruments like the kamal and astrolabe, alongside six detailed models of historic vessels representing various maritime traditions. These models, built over a year based on extensive research, are accompanied by artifacts from shipwrecks, providing tangible evidence of the cargo carried across these ancient routes.

"Spices and Wonders" also examines the cultural and religious exchanges that occurred along these trade routes, showcasing how beliefs and artistic traditions spread between civilizations. The exhibition deliberately concludes its historical narrative in the 17th century, before the significant expansion of European influence, to highlight the multicultural foundations of Indian Ocean commerce.

CCTV footage corroborated the teacher's confession, capturing violence inflicted on the pupils without justification. The assaults left the four pupils with injuries severe enough to prevent them from attending school.

A male teacher has been sentenced to two years in prison for assaulting four pupils, the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department said on Tuesday.He was found to have assaulted the four pupils in a classroom at a private school in Abu Dhabi, according to a statement by the ADJD on Tuesday.The assault resulted in the pupils suffering injuries that left them unable to attend school.

The teacher admitted the charges during the investigation and in court, the ADJD added.He admitted to “assaulting the students, claiming he did so to prevent them from causing chaos and disruption during the lesson, and in an attempt to discipline their behaviour”.

CCTV footage corroborated the confession, capturing the violence inflicted on the pupils without justification, the ADJD said.Committing the offence inside a school during lessons meant the teacher was guilty of a breach of public security and order.Protecting public order aims to safeguard the fundamental values of society, ensure the safety of its members and maintain respect for the law – principles that directly apply to the case at hand, the court heard.The teacher will be deported after serving his sentence and will have to cover all the legal costs of the case, Abu Dhabi Criminal Court ruled.The court was told the defendant’s behaviour represented a blatant breach of existing laws and regulations, underlining the necessity of firm legal enforcement to protect public safety, uphold individual rights and deter violations that subject people to harm or undermine their security and stability.Updated: October 13, 2026, 9:52 AM

articles.headline: UAE approves 2027-2029 budget with Dh292.5bn in spending
articles.dek: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion). The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed…
articles.lead: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion). The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai said on Monday.
articles.takeaway: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion).
body: The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion). The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai said on Monday.

The Cabinet also approved the 2027 budget with expenditure of Dh90.1 billion. Main sectors covered by the new federal budget include community protection and safety, the economy of the future, future-orientated education, employment and empowerment, health and quality of life, leadership, government affairs and international relations, the UAE Government Media Office said in a statement.

The budget will also focus on industry, technology, energy, infrastructure, culture, media and sports. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged … Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen,” Sheikh Mohammed said in a post on X.

The UAE last year launched its 2027-2029 budget cycle , focusing on sustainability, artificial intelligence and efficiency. It followed four consecutive cycles during which the total federal budget reached about Dh900 billion ($245 billion), officials said in July last year, adding that the cycle focuses on sectors such as education, health care, social welfare and core government services.
The UAE's economy grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war .

The non-oil sector's contribution to the country's gross domestic product during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said last week.

body: As recently as five years ago, it seemed unimaginable that electric vehicles would find any traction in the UAE. Given that fuel was relatively cheap in our region and the EV recharging infrastructure was still in its infancy, the business case for battery-powered vehicles seemed tenuous, at best.However, times change and so do buyer demands.

Petrol prices are now edging towards Dh4.50 a litre; filling up even a compact Toyota Corolla can cost more than Dh200. For drivers of larger SUVs, the expense is considerably higher – a full tank in the latest Nissan Patrol costs more than Dh400, while older models can guzzle Dh600.In this context, an EV makes financial sense, particularly for people with access to a wall-mounted home charger.

Even without one, the savings can be considerable. Depending on the vehicle's battery size, a full charge at a Dewa or Adnoc charging station typically costs little more than Dh80 ($22).Alongside rising petrol prices, the UAE's public EV charging network has continued to expand, with about 2,800 charging points across the country and more expected in the coming years.

As electric vehicles become an increasingly practical option for motorists, here are some of the best models currently available in the UAE.Under Dh100,000JAC E30X (From Dh69,995) The compact JAC E30X is one of the UAE's most affordable electric vehicles.

Although tiny in overall dimensions, the E30X's wheel-at-each-corner stance endows it with a 2,620 mm wheelbase, making it surprisingly spacious inside. With a single electric motor sending 95hp or 136hp (depending on trim level) to the front wheels, the JAC is no rocket ship, but it nevertheless feels decently zippy around town.

body: After a dream summer that saw her place fourth in the 400m hurdles at the World Athletics U20 Championships and clinch gold at the Asian Games, Emirati teenager Mariam Kareem is still trying to wrap her head around everything she has accomplished over the past couple of months.

The 18-year-old hurdler started her season running 57.39 seconds at a Grand Prix in Addis Ababa in April and finished it with a stunning 54.31s to top the podium at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, two weeks ago.
The time Kareem clocked in Japan didn’t just earn her the gold medal; it also saw her set an Asian Games record in the 400m hurdles, as well as a new Asian U20 record.
In August, Kareem, who is based in Sharjah, clocked a time of 56.27s to place fourth at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, finishing just 0.28s shy of the podium.
She felt confident she would be fast at the Asian Games the following month, but never expected she would be able to shave nearly two seconds off her time to secure the gold.
“I would say it was an unexpected thing for me,” a smiling Kareem told The National. “After the Eugene World Juniors, I had a lot of training, a lot of sessions, a lot of correction.

Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley, stated that a resolution or stabilization of conflicts will likely lead to a rebound in the UAE's IPO marketplace. articles.headline: UAE Economy Grows in First Half of 2026 Despite Regional Conflict
articles.dek: Non-oil business activity drives GDP growth, with financial and insurance sectors showing the highest expansion rates.
articles.lead: The UAE's real gross domestic product saw an annual growth of 0.4 percent in the first half of 2026, reaching Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion). This expansion was primarily fueled by non-oil business activities, even as the nation navigated the impacts of the Iran war.
articles.takeaway: Non-oil business activity drives GDP growth, with financial and insurance sectors showing the highest expansion rates.
body: The UAE's real gross domestic product saw an annual growth of 0.4 percent in the first half of 2026, reaching Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion). This expansion was primarily fueled by non-oil business activities, even as the nation navigated the impacts of the Iran war.

The contribution of the non-oil sector to the overall GDP increased to 79.2 percent during the first six months of the year, marking an 1.8 percent rise. The Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre (FCSC) highlighted this growth as a reflection of the UAE's ongoing economic diversification and the increasing significance of non-oil sectors.

Trade was the largest contributor to non-oil GDP, accounting for 16.2 percent, followed by financial and insurance services at 15.2 percent. Other key sectors included construction (13.1 percent), manufacturing (11.8 percent), and real estate (7.9 percent).

Within the non-oil economy, the financial and insurance sector experienced the most significant growth rate, expanding by 14.8 percent in the first half of 2026. Information and communication services followed with a 7.3 percent increase, while health and social work grew by 6 percent.

Despite a dip in the second quarter, where real GDP declined by 2.1 percent annually and non-oil activities contracted by 1.1 percent due to regional disruptions affecting tourism, transport, and trade, the non-oil sector has shown signs of recovery. Purchasing Managers' Index data for September indicated a stable and growing non-oil economy, suggesting a rebound from the midyear slowdown.

attribution.originalTitle: UAE economy grew in first half of 2026 despite impact of Iran war

articles.headline: UAE Teenagers Develop Feather-Based Biofertilizer
articles.dek: Three high school students have created a process to convert discarded chicken feathers into nutrient-rich fertilizer, with trials underway at farms across the UAE, Oman, and India.
articles.lead: Three enterprising teenagers from Dubai International Academy have developed a novel method to transform discarded chicken feathers into a viable biofertilizer. The project, named BioFeathers, utilizes bacteria to break down the keratin in feathers, converting them into plant nutrients. This initiative aims to reduce agricultural waste and provide a sustainable alternative for farmers.
articles.takeaway: Three high school students have created a process to convert discarded chicken feathers into nutrient-rich fertilizer, with trials underway at farms across the UAE, Oman, and India.
body: Three enterprising teenagers from Dubai International Academy have developed a novel method to transform discarded chicken feathers into a viable biofertilizer. The project, named BioFeathers, utilizes bacteria to break down the keratin in feathers, converting them into plant nutrients. This initiative aims to reduce agricultural waste and provide a sustainable alternative for farmers.

The Year 13 students, Adit Mital, Anushka Harlalka, and Maanit Misra, were inspired by the vast quantities of poultry feathers discarded globally each year, which pose environmental challenges due to their resistance to natural degradation. Their process focuses on extracting useful materials from feathers without resorting to energy-intensive methods like burning.

After months of research and laboratory experiments, including initial trials in December 2025, the team developed nine nutrient-rich formulations. Early controlled tests on bok choy and radishes showed promising results, with growth measurements indicating a 20-30% increase compared to commercial treatments, though further validation is needed.

The project has moved beyond the laboratory, with trials conducted at 16 farms and nurseries in the UAE, Oman, and India, involving over 1,200 farmers. This real-world testing helps the students understand the practical applications and requirements for scaling up their innovation. The teenagers have also filed a provisional patent application for their unique process.

Balancing their academic commitments with the demanding research, the students adapted to challenges such as limited laboratory access by conducting experiments at home. They are now planning to present their findings to Dubai Municipality and explore opportunities within the Dubai Farms program to further expand their biofertilizer initiative.

attribution.originalTitle: UAE school pupils turn feathers into fertiliser as plans to combat waste take flight

body: The UAE and Saudi Arabia have formalized an agreement to develop rail links and deepen energy cooperation. The pact, signed by UAE Minister of Investment Mohamed Alsuwaidi and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman in Riyadh, establishes a framework for connecting the countries' rail networks.

The agreement prioritizes the movement of goods and cargo across borders, with provisions for technical and economic studies to support logistics integration and improve supply chain efficiency. Both nations have committed to assessing the feasibility of linking their rail systems, reflecting a broader push for Gulf-wide economic integration.

Beyond rail infrastructure, the deal encompasses energy cooperation, including the interconnection of electricity grids and the exchange of power. Feasibility studies will be conducted to evaluate these opportunities, with coordination planned among other GCC member states.
This energy component aims to enhance system efficiency and bolster resilience across the region, aligning with the GCC's long-term connectivity objectives.

articles.headline: UAE report examines how to power AI in a water-scarce world
articles.dek: Artificial intelligence has become a major focus for global water and energy, bringing significant new demands while offering tools to improve water management, a report from the UAE Foreign Ministry has said. The repor…
articles.lead: Artificial intelligence has become a major focus for global water and energy, bringing significant new demands while offering tools to improve water management, a report from the UAE Foreign Ministry has said.
articles.takeaway: Artificial intelligence has become a major focus for global water and energy, bringing significant new demands while offering tools to improve water management, a report from the UAE Foreign Ministry has said.
body: Artificial intelligence has become a major focus for global water and energy, bringing significant new demands while offering tools to improve water management, a report from the UAE Foreign Ministry has said.

The report, Crosscurrents: Navigating the AI-Water-Energy Nexus, highlights that integrated planning and governance are essential to ensuring the technology advances sustainably without contributing to water scarcity.

"The extraordinary rise of artificial intelligence has brought with it a paradigm shift in both the nature of the global water crisis and our ability to address it," Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, said in the executive summary of the report.

EditorialAI works best when everyone is able to use it Sheikh Abdullah said that as water scarcity intensifies alongside the expansion of AI, governments and industry must manage water, energy and digital infrastructure as a single interconnected system.

The report maps water use across the AI value chain, including semiconductor manufacturing, electricity generation and cooling infrastructure, while also emphasising that indirect water use, particularly in power generation and chip production, often exceeds direct consumption at data centres themselves.

It added that policymakers have overlooked the implications of the effect of AI's rapid expansion on resources. Data centre water use is projected to about double by 2030, reaching 9.32 trillion litres.

attribution.originalTitle: UAE report examines how to power AI in a water-scarce world

articles.headline: Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation Celebrates 30 Years of Cultural Outreach
articles.dek: The Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation, established 30 years ago, has expanded from a small office to a significant cultural force, bringing arts to young people and fostering international collaborations.
articles.lead: The Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation (Admaf) is marking its 30th anniversary, reflecting on its journey from humble beginnings to a prominent cultural organization. Founded by Huda Alkhamis-Kanoo, Admaf's mission was to integrate culture into daily life and make it accessible, particularly to young people.
articles.takeaway: The Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation, established 30 years ago, has expanded from a small office to a significant cultural force, bringing arts to young people and fostering international collaborations.
body: The Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation (Admaf) is marking its 30th anniversary, reflecting on its journey from humble beginnings to a prominent cultural organization. Founded by Huda Alkhamis-Kanoo, Admaf's mission was to integrate culture into daily life and make it accessible, particularly to young people.

Initially operating from a small desk within the Kanoo Group, Admaf utilized existing cultural hubs like the Cultural Foundation and the National Theatre. Kanoo organized school bus tours, bringing students to experience concerts, operas, and ballets, aiming to broaden their horizons and provide exposure to the arts.

Early programs were self-funded by Kanoo and her husband, Mohamed Abdul Latif Kanoo, before the foundation gained traction. The initiatives expanded across schools and various locations, incorporating workshops and masterclasses that connected artists with students.

The Abu Dhabi Festival, launched in 2004, evolved from Admaf's existing work, maintaining a balance between major performances and community engagement. The festival has since hosted renowned international artists and ensembles, many of whom participated in Admaf's outreach programs.

Admaf and the Abu Dhabi Festival have also engaged in international co-commissions and exhibitions, fostering cultural exchange and providing opportunities for Emirati talent. These collaborations aim to create lasting knowledge and investment in the arts for future generations.

attribution.originalTitle: School buses to global stages: 30-year story of the Abu Dhabi Music and Arts Foundation
